rationale.text: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) classically presents as synpharyngitic hematuria — gross hematuria occurring simultaneously with (or within 1–2 days of) an upper respiratory tract infection. This differs from post-streptococcal GN, which has a 1–3 week latent period after infection.

subject: Pathology
question: What is characteristically found on immunofluorescence studies of the glomerulus in IgA nephropathy?
options: Linear IgG deposition along the GBM
Thinning of the glomerular basement membrane

rationale.text: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) = mesangial deposits of IgA on immunofluorescence — the pathognomonic finding. Linear IgG = Goodpasture syndrome. Lumpy-bumpy granular = post-infectious GN or membranoproliferative GN. Thinning of GBM = thin basement membrane nephropathy.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the most common subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by deposition of collagen in bands that divide lymph nodes into circumscribed nodules?

rationale.text: Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma, especially in young women. It is characterized by collagen bands dividing the lymph node into nodules and is usually EBV-negative. Mixed cellularity is the second most common and is EBV-positive ~70% of the time.

subject: Pathology
question: Which subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with Reed-Sternberg cells that are EBV-infected 90% of the time?

rationale.text: Lymphocyte depletion is the least common and most aggressive subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma, with Reed-Sternberg cells that are EBV-infected in ~90% of cases. It has the worst prognosis. Nodular sclerosis is typically EBV-negative. Mixed cellularity is EBV-positive ~70% of the time.

subject: Pathology
question: Which karyotype is found in a complete hydatidiform mole?

rationale.text: Complete mole has a 46,XX karyotype (diploid), formed by fertilization of an enucleated egg by two sperm (or one sperm that duplicates). Partial moles are triploid (e.g., 69,XXY). Complete moles have no fetal tissue, are associated with higher hCG, and have greater risk of choriocarcinoma than partial moles.

subject: Pathology
question: A 70-year-old man has a 3-month history of constipation and abdominal cramping. Abdominal X-ray shows 'napkin-ring' constrictions. What is the most likely diagnosis?

rationale.text: Napkin-ring (apple-core) constrictions on imaging are characteristic of distal colon (left-sided) colorectal carcinoma, which causes circumferential luminal narrowing leading to obstruction. Proximal (right-sided) colon masses usually grow as polypoid, exophytic masses and rarely cause obstruction. This is a classic pattern of left-sided colon cancer.

subject: Pathology
question: In patients with colorectal carcinoma, which factor is considered the most important prognostic determinant?

rationale.text: The depth of invasion (T stage) is the single most important prognostic factor in colorectal carcinoma, along with the presence or absence of lymph node metastases. Together, these two factors form the basis of TNM staging. CEA is useful for monitoring recurrence but not as the primary prognostic factor.

subject: Pathology
question: A 2-year-old boy is referred for co-management of a testicular mass. Microscopy shows structures resembling primitive glomeruli with central capillaries surrounded by tumor cells. Which histologic finding describes this?

rationale.text: Schiller-Duval bodies (structures resembling primitive endodermal sinuses/glomeruli) are pathognomonic of endodermal sinus tumors (yolk sac tumors), the most common testicular tumor in children under 3 years. Call-Exner bodies = granulosa cell tumors. Reinke crystalloids = Leydig cell tumors. Mallory bodies = alcoholic hepatitis.

subject: Pathology
question: Which neck cyst arises from incomplete descent of the thyroid analog from the foramen cecum, resulting in a midline cyst?

rationale.text: Thyroglossal duct cyst results from persistence of the thyroglossal duct, the tract along which the thyroid descends from the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue to its final neck position. It presents as a midline cyst that moves with swallowing. Branchial cysts arise from the 2nd branchial cleft and are lateral.

subject: Pathology
question: A patient with obstructive jaundice is found to have an enlarged, non-tender, palpable gallbladder. Which organ malignancy is most likely responsible for this finding?

rationale.text: Courvoisier sign = enlarged, non-tender, palpable gallbladder in the setting of obstructive jaundice = pancreatic carcinoma (head of pancreas) until proven otherwise. Gallbladder carcinoma causes a shrunken, fibrotic gallbladder. Liver and duodenal carcinoma do not typically cause this specific sign.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the most common type of thyroid cancer?

rationale.text: Papillary thyroid carcinoma accounts for ~85% of thyroid cancers and has an excellent prognosis. It is associated with radiation exposure, BRAF and RET/PTC mutations. Follicular carcinoma = second most common, may spread hematogenously. Medullary = C-cell origin, calcitonin-secreting, associated with MEN2. Anaplastic = most aggressive, worst prognosis.

subject: Pathology
question: A thyroid biopsy shows cells with empty-appearing nuclei with dispersed 'ground-glass' chromatin. What is the most likely histologic diagnosis?

rationale.text: Orphan Annie eye nuclei (empty-appearing nuclei with 'ground-glass' or optically clear chromatin) are the pathognomonic nuclear feature of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Other features include nuclear grooves, nuclear pseudoinclusions, psammoma bodies, and papillary architecture. These nuclei reflect finely dispersed chromatin.

subject: Pathology
question: An 80-year-old man presents with lower urinary tract symptoms, hematuria, weight loss, and back pain. Prostate carcinoma is suspected. In which zone of the prostate gland is the majority of prostate carcinoma found?

rationale.text: ~70% of prostate carcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, which can be palpated on digital rectal examination (DRE) as a hard nodule. The transition zone is the site of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). The central zone harbors few carcinomas. PSA elevation + peripheral zone lesion = high suspicion for prostate cancer.

subject: Pathology
question: What is considered the mainstay of diagnosis for syphilis?

rationale.text: Serology is the mainstay of syphilis diagnosis, including nontreponemal tests (VDRL, RPR — screening) and treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TPPA — confirmatory). Dark-field microscopy can visualize Treponema pallidum directly in primary chancre exudate but is not widely available. Culture of T. pallidum is not practical.

subject: Pathology
question: A patient diagnosed with pancreatic adenocarcinoma develops DVT in the left leg that spontaneously resolves, only to reappear in the right leg. What is this migratory thrombophlebitis called?

rationale.text: Trousseau syndrome (migratory thrombophlebitis) is a paraneoplastic phenomenon classically associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, caused by tumor-induced hypercoagulability. Leser-Trelat sign = sudden appearance of multiple seborrheic keratoses in GI malignancy. Chvostek sign = facial muscle twitch from hypocalcemia. Acanthosis nigricans = GI or other visceral malignancy.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following autoimmune diseases does NOT develop in association with Hashimoto thyroiditis?

rationale.text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is not an autoimmune disease and does not cluster with Hashimoto thyroiditis. Hashimoto thyroiditis is associated with other autoimmune diseases: Type 1 DM, autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison's), SLE, myasthenia gravis, and Sjögren syndrome (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy clustering).

subject: Pathology
question: Deficiency of which substance leads to degeneration of both ascending and descending spinal tracts, causing subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord?

rationale.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency → subacute combined degeneration: demyelination of dorsal columns (posterior) and corticospinal tracts (lateral) → sensory ataxia + spastic paraparesis. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency = Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Vitamin A deficiency = night blindness, Bitot spots. Vitamin E deficiency = spinocerebellar degeneration.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the most common cause of myocarditis?

rationale.text: Viral infections — primarily Coxsackie virus A and B — are the most common causes of myocarditis worldwide. Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) is the most common cause in endemic regions of South America. Alcohol causes dilated cardiomyopathy, not myocarditis per se. ACS causes ischemic necrosis.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death?

rationale.text: Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death, responsible for up to 80% of cases. Fatal ventricular arrhythmias (VF/VT) arise from ischemic myocardium. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common cause in young athletes. Aortic stenosis and rheumatic heart disease cause SCD much less frequently.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the most common mechanism by which pathogenic organisms gain access to the lung to cause lung abscesses?

rationale.text: Aspiration is the most common mechanism for lung abscess formation. Risk factors include: suppressed cough reflexes, dysphagia, protracted vomiting, and poor dental hygiene. Aspirated material more commonly reaches the right lung (more vertical main bronchus). Septic emboli from endocarditis are another important mechanism.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following is NOT true regarding lung abscesses?
options: More commonly occur in the left lung

rationale.text: Lung abscesses from aspiration are more common in the RIGHT lung because the right main bronchus is more vertical and has a wider lumen than the left. Foul-smelling sputum is characteristic of anaerobic infection. Clubbing of fingers (not toes) may develop with chronic lung abscess. 'More common in the left lung' is NOT true.

subject: Pathology
question: What is considered the earliest lesion in Crohn's disease?

rationale.text: Aphthous ulcers are the earliest lesions in Crohn's disease, forming over lymphoid follicles in the bowel mucosa. As the disease progresses: ulcers coalesce → cobblestoning → crypt abscesses → transmural inflammation → granulomas (in ~35%) → creeping fat (mesenteric fat wrapping). All of these features can be present, but aphthous ulcers appear first.

subject: Pathology
question: Which pneumoconiosis is characteristically associated with eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes on chest radiograph?

rationale.text: Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes is a classic radiographic sign of silicosis, caused by inhalation of silicon dioxide (quartz). Silicosis also increases the risk of TB (silicotuberculosis) and lung cancer. Asbestosis causes lower lobe fibrosis and pleural plaques. CWP causes Caplan lesions in rheumatoid arthritis patients.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following is TRUE in patients who are heavy smokers AND have heavy asbestos exposure?
options: Higher risk of developing lung cancer
Lower risk of dying from lung cancer
No additional risk beyond asbestos alone

rationale.text: Smokers with heavy asbestos exposure have a synergistically higher risk of developing lung cancer (multiplicative, not additive). However, there is no increased risk of developing mesothelioma in patients who both smoke and are exposed to asbestos — mesothelioma risk from asbestos is not synergized by smoking.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following is NOT found in patients with prostate cancer?

rationale.text: Prostate cancer characteristically produces osteoBLASTIC (sclerotic/bone-forming) metastases to bone, NOT osteoclastic (lytic) metastases. This is the opposite of most other cancers (e.g., breast, kidney, lung, thyroid cause lytic metastases). Prostate cancer spreads hematogenously to bones, especially the axial skeleton and femur.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following testicular tumors carries the best prognosis?

rationale.text: Seminomas have the best prognosis among testicular germ cell tumors because they are both radiosensitive and chemosensitive. They tend to spread via lymphatics and present at a lower stage. Yolk sac tumors have favorable outcomes in children but worse prognosis in adults. Embryonal carcinoma is more aggressive.

subject: Pathology
question: The appearance of gas-forming bacteria such as Clostridia in the gallbladder may result in which type of cholecystitis?

rationale.text: Emphysematous cholecystitis is caused by gas-forming organisms (Clostridia, E. coli) in the gallbladder wall, producing gas visible on imaging. It occurs more commonly in diabetic and elderly patients and carries a higher risk of perforation. Gas in the gallbladder wall or lumen on CT is the diagnostic finding.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following does NOT contribute to the formation of cholesterol gallstones?

rationale.text: Cholesterol gallstone formation requires: (1) bile supersaturation with cholesterol, (2) gallbladder hypomotility reducing bile clearance, and (3) cholesterol crystal nucleation. Mucus HYPERsecretion (not hyposecretion) promotes stone formation by trapping crystals. Hyposecretion of mucus does NOT contribute.

subject: Pathology
question: Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite causing Chagas disease, is transmitted to humans by which vector?

rationale.text: T. cruzi is transmitted by triatomine bugs (reduviid/kissing bugs) through their feces deposited near the bite wound. Tsetse flies transmit T. brucei (African sleeping sickness). Toxoplasma cysts are acquired through undercooked meat. Cryptosporidium/Giardia cysts are waterborne.

subject: Pathology
question: Exposure to which environmental carcinogen is most directly associated with the development of skin cancer?

rationale.text: Arsenic exposure causes skin cancer (squamous cell carcinoma, Bowen disease, and arsenical keratoses). Benzene → acute myeloid leukemia. Cadmium → prostate carcinoma. Vinyl chloride → hepatic angiosarcoma. Arsenic also causes peripheral vascular disease and causes characteristic Mees' lines on fingernails.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following cancers most commonly causes SIADH as a paraneoplastic syndrome?

rationale.text: Small cell lung carcinoma is the most common cause of SIADH as a paraneoplastic syndrome (ectopic ADH production). It also causes ectopic ACTH → Cushing syndrome. Renal cell carcinoma → hypercalcemia (PTHrP) + polycythemia (EPO). Cerebellar hemangioblastoma → polycythemia. Breast cancer → hypercalcemia.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following can cause pseudotumor cerebri, presenting with headache, vomiting, and blurred vision from elevated intracranial pressure?

rationale.text: Acute vitamin A toxicity causes pseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension), mimicking a brain tumor with elevated ICP but no mass lesion. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and Bitot spots. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the most common monoclonal immunoglobulin produced in multiple myeloma?

rationale.text: IgG is the most common monoclonal protein (M-protein) in multiple myeloma (~55%), followed by IgA (~25%). IgM is characteristic of Waldenström macroglobulinemia, not multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma cell neoplasm producing excess immunoglobulin, causing bone lesions, hypercalcemia, renal failure, and infections.

subject: Pathology
question: An elderly woman presents with tense bullae on the flexor surfaces of her forearms, axillae, and groin. Immunofluorescence shows linear deposition of complement along the dermoepidermal junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

rationale.text: Bullous pemphigoid = tense bullae in elderly + anti-hemidesmosome antibodies (IgG) + linear IF deposition at the dermoepidermal junction (subepidermal blister). Pemphigus vulgaris = flaccid intraepidermal bullae + anti-desmoglein IgG + reticular IF pattern on keratinocyte membranes. Dermatitis herpetiformis = IgA deposits at dermal papillae tips.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the most significant risk factor for the development of renal cell carcinoma?

rationale.text: Tobacco smoking is the most significant modifiable risk factor for renal cell carcinoma (RCC), increasing risk 2-fold. Other risk factors: obesity, hypertension, Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL mutation → clear cell RCC). Vinyl chloride exposure → hepatic angiosarcoma. RCC arises from proximal tubular cells and is associated with clear cell, papillary, and chromophobe subtypes.

subject: Pathology
question: A female patient is described as having a unilateral, erythematous, scaly-crusted lesion involving the nipple and areola. Which breast pathology does this represent?

rationale.text: Paget disease of the nipple is an extension of DCIS through the ductal system into the nipple skin, producing a unilateral eczematous erythematous scaly lesion. Large neoplastic Paget cells infiltrate the epidermis. It is a rare but important breast carcinoma presentation. Inflammatory breast carcinoma causes skin erythema and peau d'orange from dermal lymphatic invasion.

subject: Pathology
question: A patient presents with pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules and plaques on the wrists and oral mucosa. Lacy white lines are noted on the buccal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?

rationale.text: Lichen planus = the 6 P's: Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar, Papules, and Plaques. Wickham striae (lacy white lines) are a characteristic finding on skin and buccal mucosa. Psoriasis = salmon-colored plaques with silver scales. Pemphigus = flaccid bullae. Dermatitis herpetiformis = symmetric vesicles on extensor surfaces.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following skin disorders is strongly associated with celiac disease?

rationale.text: Dermatitis herpetiformis is a cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease. IgA antibodies to dietary gluten cross-react with reticulin in the skin → itchy vesicular eruption on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). Skin biopsy shows IgA deposits at the dermal papillary tips. Both DH and celiac disease improve on a gluten-free diet.

subject: Pathology
question: Which type of renal stone forms specifically after infection with urea-splitting bacteria such as Proteus?

rationale.text: Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) stones form when urea-splitting bacteria (Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas) convert urea → ammonia → alkaline urine → struvite precipitates. These stones can fill the entire renal pelvis, forming staghorn calculi. They are more common in women due to higher UTI rates.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the most common type of renal calculus?

rationale.text: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type of renal calculi (~70–80%), often mixed with calcium phosphate. They appear on CT (radiopaque) and are associated with hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, and hypocitraturia. Struvite = infection stones. Uric acid = radiolucent, associated with gout. Cystine = rare, autosomal recessive cystinuria.

subject: Pathology
question: A patient has a rare pancreatic endocrine neoplasm associated with diabetes mellitus, a characteristic migratory skin rash, and anemia. Which type of pancreatic tumor is responsible?

rationale.text: Alpha cell tumors (glucagonomas) present with the classic triad: diabetes mellitus (glucagon opposes insulin), necrolytic migratory erythema (characteristic rash), and anemia. Elevated plasma glucagon confirms the diagnosis. Delta cell tumors → diabetes + cholelithiasis + steatorrhea + hypochlorhydria. VIPomas → WDHA syndrome.

subject: Pathology
question: The 'rule of 10s' in pheochromocytoma states several features. Which of the following is NOT part of this rule?

rationale.text: The rule of 10s: 10% extraadrenal, 10% bilateral, 10% ARE biologically malignant (not 'not malignant'), and 10% are not associated with hypertension. The statement '10% are NOT biologically malignant' is INCORRECT — the correct statement is that 10% ARE malignant. The other three options accurately reflect the rule of 10s.

subject: Pathology
question: Which MEN syndrome is NOT associated with pheochromocytoma?

rationale.text: MEN1 (Parathyroid + Pancreas + Pituitary) is NOT associated with pheochromocytoma. MEN2A (medullary thyroid CA + pheochromocytoma + parathyroid hyperplasia) and MEN2B (medullary thyroid CA + pheochromocytoma + mucosal neuromas) are BOTH associated with pheochromocytoma via RET proto-oncogene mutations.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the most commonly affected joint in calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition disease?

rationale.text: The knees are the most commonly affected joints in CPPD (pseudogout). CPPD results from calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition in articular cartilage, causing chondrocalcinosis visible on X-ray. Gout (monosodium urate crystals) classically affects the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra). CPPD crystals are rhomboid-shaped and positively birefringent.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the most characteristic morphological feature of apoptosis?

rationale.text: Chromatin condensation (nuclear pyknosis, then karyorrhexis) is the most characteristic and specific feature of apoptosis, resulting from endonuclease activation and DNA fragmentation at internucleosomal sites. Cell shrinkage, apoptotic body formation, and phagocytosis also occur in apoptosis but are less specific or occur sequentially after chromatin condensation.

subject: Pathology
question: Which indoor air pollutant is considered the number one cause of lung cancer in non-smokers?

rationale.text: Radon is an indoor air pollutant and the leading cause of lung cancer in non-smokers. It is an odorless radioactive gas that accumulates in basements and poorly ventilated spaces. Carbon monoxide is an outdoor air pollutant. Formaldehyde and bioaerosols are indoor pollutants but are not associated with lung cancer causation in non-smokers.

subject: Pathology
question: A patient presents with cherry-red discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes after acute exposure to an air pollutant. Which substance is responsible?

rationale.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning = cherry-red skin and mucous membranes from increased carboxyhemoglobin (CO has 200× higher affinity for hemoglobin than O₂). CO is produced by incomplete combustion. Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) causes anion gap metabolic acidosis with oxalate crystals → renal failure. Ozone causes airway irritation and chest discomfort.

subject: Pathology
question: A 40/F comes to you complaining of easy fatigability. On PE, she is pale and slightly tachycardic. On a CBC, she has a low hemoglobin, low MCV and normal reticulocyte count. Which of the following is the likely cause of her anemia?

rationale.text: Iron deficiency anemia is microcytic (low MCV) with normal or low reticulocyte count. Vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies are macrocytic. Vitamin K deficiency affects clotting, not RBC production.

subject: Pathology
question: Which one of the following pathological abnormality DOES NOT manifest with chronic cough of more than 8 weeks duration?

rationale.text: Laryngeal edema is usually acute (e.g., anaphylaxis, intubation) and not a typical cause of chronic cough. Postnasal drip, GERD, and chronic bronchitis are common causes of chronic cough.

subject: Pathology
question: PAS-positive cytoplasmic inclusions known as Bunina bodies are:

rationale.text: Bunina bodies are small eosinophilic intraneuronal inclusions in ALS, considered remnants of autophagic vacuoles. They are PAS-positive.

subject: Pathology
question: A two-year old female presented with a defect in her lower anterior abdomen wall since birth. On physical examination, you noted a globular soft tissue protrusion from the defect. In the inferior aspect of which were two openings where urine dribbled continuously. What is the most likely diagnosis?

rationale.text: Bladder exstrophy presents with a lower abdominal wall defect, exposed bladder mucosa, and continuous urine dribbling from the ureteral orifices. Persistent urachus also causes umbilical urine drainage but lacks the abdominal wall defect.

subject: Pathology
question: In which of the following dopamine tract would antagonism of dopamine lead to Parkinson-like symptoms?

rationale.text: Antagonism of dopamine in the nigrostriatal tract leads to extrapyramidal symptoms (Parkinson-like). The mesolimbic tract is involved in positive symptoms of schizophrenia; the tuberoinfundibular tract regulates prolactin.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following population groups is generally protected against myocardial infarction?

rationale.text: Women of reproductive age are relatively protected against MI due to estrogen's cardioprotective effects. The risk increases after menopause.

subject: Pathology
question: A 25-year old sales lady stepped into the elevator full of people with influenza, coughing and sneezing. The viral particles which she inhaled attached to her respiratory epithelium. Which immune cell is MOST likely to rapidly destroy the virally infected cells?

rationale.text: NK cells are part of the innate immune system and can rapidly kill virus-infected cells without prior sensitization, by recognizing reduced MHC class I expression.

subject: Pathology
question: Tita Lydia has been diagnosed to have Congestive Heart Failure for the past 3 years. Upon review of her history, it was noted that she developed productive rust-colored sputum for the past 2 months. Her doctor requested sputum cytology which revealed numerous hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Which subcellular structures found in macrophages explains the accumulation of this pigment?

rationale.text: Hemosiderin accumulates in macrophages within lysosomes after phagocytosis and breakdown of red blood cells. This is seen in pulmonary hemosiderosis (e.g., in CHF).

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following will increase stroke volume?

rationale.text: A decrease in end-systolic volume (i.e., reduced afterload or increased contractility) increases stroke volume. Decreased afterload and increased preload both increase stroke volume.

subject: Pathology
question: Isabel was admitted for hyponatremia. About 48 hours after rapid and aggressive correction of her hyponatremia, she developed acute paralysis, difficulty speaking, and difficulty swallowing. Which of the following is the most likely pathology behind her new symptoms?
options: Demyelination due to toxic chemicals used in cleaning liquids
Autoimmune response directed against the myelin sheath
Myelin loss throughout the white matter
Loss of myelin in the basis pontis and pontine tegmentum

rationale.text: Rapid correction of hyponatremia can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis), with demyelination in the basis pontis and pontine tegmentum.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following features of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus is least likely?
options: It affects predominantly women of child-bearing age
SLE affects any age group especially during childhood
Affects every organ of the body especially skin, kidney, joints, and serosal membranes
It is chronic, remitting and relapsing, often febrile

rationale.text: While SLE can occur in children, it is not especially a disease of childhood; it most commonly presents in women of child-bearing age.

subject: Pathology
question: Which risk factor with both Trisomy 13 and 18, and Trisomy 21?

rationale.text: Advanced maternal age is the most significant risk factor for trisomies 13, 18, and 21, due to increased meiotic nondisjunction.

subject: Pathology
question: The most characteristic lesions of SLE result from immune complex deposition in the following areas, which one is least?

rationale.text: Immune complex deposition in SLE commonly affects kidney, blood vessels, and skin. Bone involvement is not a characteristic site of immune complex deposition.

subject: Pathology
question: A 62 year old jeepney driver developed an acute cough productive of phlegm. His doctor said the pathology could be in his lower lung airways. Which of the following could this be?

rationale.text: Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchial tubes (lower airways) and commonly presents with acute cough productive of phlegm. Pneumonia affects alveoli, tracheitis and sinusitis are upper airway.

subject: Pathology
question: Which pathological abnormality does not manifest with chronic cough of more than 8 weeks duration?

rationale.text: Laryngeal edema is typically acute (e.g., anaphylaxis, intubation) and not a cause of chronic cough. Postnasal drip, chronic bronchitis, and GERD are common causes of chronic cough.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following general features of autoimmune diseases is least likely?
options: Autoimmune disease are chronic with relapse and remissions
Autoimmune diseases tend to follow an acute course of illness with tendency to progression in the future
Clinical and pathologic manifestations are determined by the nature of underlying immune response
Damage caused by autoimmune diseases is progressive

rationale.text: Autoimmune diseases are typically chronic, not acute. They often have relapsing-remitting courses or progressive damage, but not an acute course with future progression.

subject: Pathology
question: Your grandmother who is 95 years old accidentally touches a pot of boiling water. The skin of her finger in 2 hours then revealed marked erythema and small blisters. This event has led to which inflammatory response?

rationale.text: A burn causing erythema and small blisters is a serous inflammation (thin, watery fluid accumulation). Purulent involves pus, granulomatous involves granulomas, fibrinous involves fibrin.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following lung pathology can give rise to pulmonary embolism?

rationale.text: Pulmonary embolism arises from defects in the pulmonary vasculature (e.g., thrombosis, embolism). Chest wall, airways, or parenchymal defects do not directly cause PE.

subject: Pathology
question: How does suicidal attempts by ingestion of harsh chemicals cause acute gastritis?
options: Decreased prostaglandins which stimulates defense mechanism
Due to direct injury to mucosal epithelial and stromal cells

rationale.text: Ingestion of harsh chemicals causes acute gastritis by direct corrosive injury to mucosal epithelial and stromal cells. Decreased prostaglandins/bicarbonate are mechanisms of other types of gastropathy.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following statements regarding pheochromocytoma is TRUE?
options: Only 10% of adrenal pheochromocytomas are biologically malignant
A germline mutation is present in all pheochromocytomas
Adrenal pheochromocytomas are always associated with hypertension

rationale.text: About 10% of adrenal pheochromocytomas are biologically malignant (metastasize). Germline mutations are not in all cases; ~10% are not associated with hypertension; bilaterality is not necessarily malignant.

subject: Pathology
question: What morphological changes will be MOST likely expected to find in a patient with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis?
options: Preserved volume of the upper neurons along the corticospinal tract
Thinning of the anterior roots of the spinal cord due to loss of lower motor neuron fibers
Hypertrophic precentral motor gyrus in the cortex to compensate for lower motor neuron loss
Relatively preserved number of anterior horn neurons throughout the length of the spinal cord

rationale.text: ALS causes degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons. Thinning of anterior roots (loss of lower motor neuron fibers) and atrophy of the precentral gyrus are characteristic.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following statements would consistently describe the extent of vessel involvement in the formation of atherosclerotic lesions?
options: Due to consistent degree of atherosclerotic burden in affected vessels, the severity of the disease is one arterial distribution usually predicts the severity in another
The most extensively involved vessels include the coronary and popliteal arteries, internal carotid arteries, and vessels in the circle of Willis
In humans, the thoracic aorta is typically involved to a much greater degree than the lower abdominal aorta
Vessels of the upper extremities, mesenteric and renal arteries often develop atheromatous plaques

rationale.text: The most extensively involved vessels are the lower abdominal aorta, coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, internal carotid arteries, and circle of Willis. Severity in one distribution does not always predict another.

subject: Pathology
question: Imaging studies showed a connection from the bladder to the umbilicus in female infant who often wet the top of her diaper. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

rationale.text: A persistent urachus is a connection between the bladder and umbilicus, causing urine leakage from the umbilicus. Exstrophy is a bladder wall defect; vitelline duct remnant connects to the ileum.

subject: Pathology
question: Tita Luz, 55 years old, comes to your clinic for undocumented fever, and productive cough with yellowish sputum of 2 days duration. Persistent pertinent findings in her physical examination reveal slight tachypnea and audible crackles at the lung bases. Chest radiographs show patchy infiltrates in both lungs. Which of the following inflammatory cells will MOST likely be seen increased when a sample of respiratory sputum is sent for analysis?

rationale.text: Acute bacterial pneumonia is characterized by neutrophilic infiltration of alveoli, giving purulent sputum. Macrophages are more prominent in chronic inflammation.

subject: Pathology
question: A 70 year-old man with hematuria underwent cystoscopy. An erythematous area was biopsied, showing flat lesions composed of cells in mid to upper epithelium with high cytologic grade. There was no invasion in the lamina propria noted. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

rationale.text: Urothelial carcinoma in situ (CIS) is a flat, high-grade lesion confined to the epithelium without lamina propria invasion. T1 would involve lamina propria; AML is a hematologic malignancy.

subject: Pathology
question: So-called “smudge cells” are seen in which one?

rationale.text: Smudge cells (basket cells) are characteristic of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) due to fragile lymphocytes that rupture during smear preparation.

subject: Pathology
question: Which step in the physical examination of the patient would DOUBT the pathology of a patient in respiratory distress?
options: Patient uses his accessory muscles of respiration
Patient is unable to complete a sentence in conversation

rationale.text: Severe kyphoscoliosis can cause restrictive lung disease and respiratory distress. Excessive phlegm, accessory muscle use, and inability to complete sentences are all signs of respiratory distress.

subject: Pathology
question: What are these morphologically atypical keratinocytes described as enlarged cells with eccentric, pyknotic nuclei surrounded by a perinuclear halo, found in human papilloma virus infection?

rationale.text: Koilocytes are the hallmark of HPV infection: enlarged cells with eccentric, pyknotic nuclei and perinuclear halos. Michaelis-Gutman bodies are seen in malakoplakia; Schiller-Duval in yolk sac tumors.

subject: Pathology
question: Once bacteria enter the body, leukocytes leave the vasculature then migrate towards the site of bacterial inoculation. Which of the following substances is MOST likely responsible for the movement of the said leukocytes?

rationale.text: Chemokines are the primary chemoattractants directing leukocyte migration to sites of infection. C5a (not C3a) is also a chemoattractant; histamine and prostaglandins mediate vasodilation and vascular permeability.

subject: Pathology
question: If ACTH is elevated and completely insensitive to low or high doses of dexamethasone, what is the probable cause of Cushing Syndrome?

rationale.text: Ectopic ACTH secretion (e.g., from small cell lung cancer) is not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone. Pituitary adenomas are usually suppressible; adrenal tumors and exogenous steroids cause low ACTH.

subject: Pathology
question: Glycogen storage diseases come from a hereditary deficiency of one of the enzymes involved in the synthesis or sequential degradation of glycogen. In the hepatic form of this group of diseases, the liver cells store glycogen because of the deficiency of which enzymes?

rationale.text: Von Gierke disease (hepatic form) is due to deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase, causing glycogen accumulation in liver. Lysosomal acid maltase deficiency causes Pompe (muscle); muscle phosphorylase causes McArdle.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the MOST likely pathology behind rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with concomitant diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage?
options: Presence of circulating anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies
Pathology is currently unknown or is idiopathic
Renal pathology secondary to adaptive changes from systemic disease
Diffuse inflammatory response after a severe or systemic infection

rationale.text: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM antibodies) causes rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage. It is a type II hypersensitivity reaction.

subject: Pathology
question: Presence of atherosclerotic plaques makes a person susceptible to the following, which one is LEAST likely susceptible?

rationale.text: Atherosclerosis predisposes to atheroembolism, aneurysm formation, and thrombosis. Valvular heart disease (e.g., rheumatic, calcific) is not directly caused by atherosclerosis.

subject: Pathology
question: What morphological changes will be MOST likely expected to find in a patient with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)?
options: Thinning of the anterior roots of the spinal cord due to loss of lower motor neuron fibers
Presence of intracellular neurofibrillary tangles in neurons
Accumulation of Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra

rationale.text: ALS is characterized by loss of both upper and lower motor neurons. Thinning of anterior roots (lower motor neuron loss) is a key finding. Neurofibrillary tangles (Alzheimer's), peripheral demyelination (GBS), and Lewy bodies (Parkinson's) are not features.

subject: Pathology
question: A 40/F comes to you complaining of easy fatigability. On PE she is pale and slightly tachycardic. On a CBC she has a low hemoglobin, low MCV and normal reticulocyte count. Which is the likely cause of her anemia?

rationale.text: Low MCV (microcytic) with low hemoglobin and normal reticulocyte count is classic for iron deficiency anemia. B12 and folate deficiencies are macrocytic; vitamin K affects clotting.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following have panmyelosis?

rationale.text: Panmyelosis (trilineage hyperplasia) is characteristic of polycythemia vera. Multiple myeloma affects plasma cells; hairy cell leukemia involves B-cells; acute megakaryoblastic leukemia affects megakaryoblasts.

subject: Pathology
question: Astrocytic tumors in which predominant neoplastic astrocyte shows a brightly eosinophilic cell body from which emanate abundant, stout processes is a/an ___ astrocytoma.

rationale.text: Gemistocytic astrocytoma is characterized by abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and stout processes. Pilocytic has bipolar 'hairlike' processes; diffuse has fibrillary background; anaplastic has mitoses and pleomorphism.

subject: Pathology
question: Capillaries with fenestrated endothelium have gaps between endothelial cells but the basement membrane is still continuous. In which structures are these NOT found?

rationale.text: Fenestrated capillaries are found in endocrine glands, renal glomeruli, and intestinal villi. The blood-brain barrier has continuous (non-fenestrated) capillaries.

subject: Pathology
question: A 55 year old factory worker consulted the clinic because of increasing dyspnea without cough or sputum production. He had been experiencing these for 6 months. His breath sounds were reduced in all lung fields. CXR showed dense brightly attenuated pleural mass encasing most of his left lung. Pleural biopsy specimen showed spindle and cuboidal cells invading adipose tissue. Which is the MOST likely etiologic factor in the pathogenesis of this mass?

rationale.text: A dense pleural mass encasing the lung with spindle and cuboidal cells is malignant mesothelioma, strongly associated with asbestos exposure. Silica causes silicosis (nodular), coal dust causes CWP, bird droppings cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

subject: Pathology
question: Evelyn, 33 yo, consulted for dizziness, nausea and vomiting especially in the morning. A pregnancy test is done with a positive result. She is then referred to an OBGYNE who had her fetal UTZ done at 13 weeks AOG with her uterus measuring 8x5x4 cm. She delivers her first baby full term 8 months after via spontaneous vaginal delivery. Her uterus during delivery measures 33 x 17 x 11 cm. Which cellular process contributed largely to her increase in uterine size?

rationale.text: Uterine growth during pregnancy is primarily due to hypertrophy of myometrial smooth muscle cells (and some hyperplasia). Vascular and endometrial changes are secondary.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following is the cause of the EARLY clinical manifestations of CHF?

rationale.text: Early CHF manifests with poor tissue perfusion (fatigue, weakness) due to reduced cardiac output. Low oxygen saturation is a later finding; vascular and endometrial changes are unrelated.

subject: Pathology
question: Which condition manifests with normal breathing, with recurrent episodes of dyspnea triggered by upper respiratory infection and allergens?

rationale.text: Asthma is characterized by recurrent episodes of dyspnea, often triggered by allergens or infections, with normal breathing between episodes. Pneumonia and fibrosis are more continuous; COPD is usually persistent.

subject: Pathology
question: A student researcher injected a chemical into his skin. Next day, he noticed an erythematous indurated area forming around the site. After two days, there was even bigger induration of about 10mm diameter. Histologically, there were many positive lymphocytes present. Which of the following reactions is MOST consistent with this appearance?

rationale.text: Delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) is mediated by T lymphocytes and takes 24-72 hours to develop, with induration and erythema. Arthus (Type III) is antibody-mediated; localized anaphylaxis (Type I) is immediate; GVHD is a transplant complication.

subject: Pathology
question: Barr body is an inactivated X chromosome seen upon microscopic examination of the neutrophilic nuclei in females but is absent in males. Which of the following forms of RNA plays a role in the formation of this Barr Body?

rationale.text: Long noncoding RNA (lncRNA), specifically XIST, is responsible for X-chromosome inactivation and Barr body formation. mRNA, miRNA, and tRNA are not directly involved.

subject: Pathology
question: A 65 year old teacher has had chronic non-productive cough for 6 months with associated weight loss. She is a non-smoker. Physical examination done on her was unremarkable, but her chest x-ray showed a right peripheral subpleural mass. A fine needle aspiration was done and she underwent right lower lobectomy. She was placed on immunotherapy. Which of the following neoplasms did she MOST likely have?

rationale.text: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer in non-smokers and typically presents as a peripheral mass. Squamous and small cell are more central and smoking-related; hamartoma is benign.

subject: Pathology
question: What could be an underlying pathologic disease which can cause the patient’s mediastinum to shift from right to left?

rationale.text: Distal acinar (paraseptal) emphysema can cause large bullae that shift the mediastinum. Bronchiectasis, asthma, and centriacinar emphysema do not typically cause significant mediastinal shift.

subject: Pathology
question: The following are contributory factors to the development of secondary hypertension, which one of the following is a LEAST likely factor?

rationale.text: Obesity is a risk factor for primary (essential) hypertension, not secondary. Pheochromocytoma, primary aldosteronism, and renal artery stenosis are secondary causes.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the MOST likely pathology behind rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with concomitant diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage?
options: Pathology is currently unknown or is idiopathic
Presence of circulating anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies
Diffuse inflammatory response after a severe or systemic infection
Renal pathology secondary to adaptive changes from systemic disease

rationale.text: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM antibodies) is the classic cause of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage.

subject: Pathology
question: Which lung problem does not cause hemoptysis due to erosions to blood vessel vasculature?

rationale.text: Pneumothorax (air in pleural space) does not typically cause hemoptysis. Tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism (with infarction), and bronchogenic carcinoma can all erode vessels and cause hemoptysis.

subject: Pathology
question: A patient presents with thrombocytopenia, anemia, strokes but normal PT, low D-dimer. Which is MOST likely?

rationale.text: TTP presents with thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, neurologic symptoms (strokes), fever, and renal dysfunction. PT is normal, D-dimer is low (unlike DIC). HUS has more renal involvement; ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia.

subject: Pathology
question: In which of the following conditions will you expect to find distinct crescents formed by proliferation of parietal cells and migration of monocytes and macrophages in the urinary space in light microscopy?

rationale.text: Crescents in Bowman's space are the hallmark of rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis. Dense-deposit has intramembranous deposits; MPGN has tram-track; FSGS has segmental sclerosis.

subject: Pathology
question: Lolo Pedro has been experiencing increasing bouts of knee pain during ambulation for the past 10 years. x-ray findings show that the knee joint surfaces are eroded and joint space narrowed. There is also loss of:

rationale.text: Osteoarthritis involves loss of articular cartilage and decreased hyaluronan in synovial fluid. Fibronectin, elastin, and laminin are not the primary components lost.

subject: Pathology
question: Which of the following statements regarding thyroid nodule is TRUE?
options: Nodules in females are more likely to be neoplastic than those in males
Multiple nodules, in general, are more likely to be neoplastic than solitary nodules
Nodules in younger patients are more likely to be benign than those in older patients
Functional nodules that take up radioactive iodine are more benign than malignant

rationale.text: Hot (functional) nodules that take up radioactive iodine are almost always benign. Malignancy is more common in males, solitary nodules, and younger patients.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the MAIN pathology involved in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)?
options: Preferential damage to myelin with relative preservation of axons, leading to poor transmission of electrical impulses
Progressive loss of upper motor neurons in the cerebral cortex and lower motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem
Protein accumulation and aggregation, mitochondrial abnormalities, and neuronal loss in the substantia nigra
Characterized by cytoplasmic inclusions of alpha-synuclein in oligodendrocytes and degeneration of white matter

rationale.text: ALS is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive loss of both upper and lower motor neurons. Myelin damage (MS), substantia nigra loss (Parkinson's), and alpha-synuclein oligodendrocyte inclusions (MSA) are not features.

subject: Pathology
question: During pre-employment screening, chest radiograph of 35-year old Albert shows a 3.5 cm nodule in the middle lobe of the right lung. The nodule is resected and sectioning shows a sharply circumscribed mass with a soft white center. Which pathologic process MOST likely explains this nodule?

rationale.text: A sharply circumscribed mass with a soft white center (caseous necrosis) is characteristic of a tuberculous granuloma (tuberculoma). Coagulative necrosis is ischemic; liquefactive is abscess/brain; gangrenous is ischemic with superinfection.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 1 - A 10-year old boy staying in the garbage mountain of Tondo, developed diarrhea for more than a week of about 5-6 times/ day. Stool was blood streaked and associated with mild abdominal tenderness. Patient also has intestinal tuberculosis. What organism is involved in this case?

rationale.text: Shigella is a common cause of bloody diarrhea (dysentery) in children in resource-limited settings. Giardia causes non-bloody diarrhea; Entamoeba can cause bloody diarrhea but is less common in this setting; Salmonella typhi causes typhoid fever.

subject: Pathology
question: What microscopic finding is NOT found in this case?
options: Mononuclear infiltrates extending to the lamina propria

rationale.text: Stricture formation is a chronic complication of intestinal tuberculosis, not an acute finding. Shigellosis causes acute inflammation with mononuclear infiltrates, epithelial disruption, and organisms in the lamina propria.

subject: Pathology
question: Why is the dysentery bloody?
options: Disease can cause fragility of blood vessels
Disease involves erosions of intestinal tissues
Organism is highly virulent and can destroy colonic mucosa

rationale.text: Shigella is highly virulent, invades and destroys colonic mucosa, causing ulceration and bloody diarrhea. Direct blood vessel destruction is not the primary mechanism.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 2 - A 60-year old male, oftentimes develop epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting. He decided to consult his doctor because of the said symptoms. The doctor diagnosed him as having 'acute gastritis' and requested for a CBC. The complete blood count results showed absence of neutrophils. The better diagnostic term applied is ___?

rationale.text: Gastropathy is used when there is gastric mucosal injury without significant inflammation (i.e., absence of neutrophils). Acute gastritis implies neutrophilic inflammation.

subject: Pathology
question: Which one of the following does not cause gastric injury or dysfunction?

rationale.text: Yogurt is generally protective for the gastric mucosa (probiotics). Stress, NSAIDs, and bile reflux can all cause gastric injury (gastropathy/gastritis).

subject: Pathology
question: Which one of the following is NOT involved in the pathogenesis of Acute Gastritis causing damage to gastric mucosa?
options: Inhibition of cyclooxygenase dependent synthesis of prostaglandin
Inhibition of gastric bicarbonate transporters by H. pylori
Decreased oxygen delivery for those at high altitudes

rationale.text: Increased mucin and bicarbonate secretions are protective, not damaging. Inhibition of prostaglandins, inhibition of bicarbonate transporters, and decreased oxygen delivery all contribute to gastric mucosal injury.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 3 – A 50-year old OCW visited a remote provincial town and drank water from a nearby store. Over the next 2 days, he developed severe profuse diarrhea, rice water stools, became dehydrated, thus was rushed to an emergency room for intravenous hydration. What is the patient having?

rationale.text: Rice-water stools and severe dehydration are classic for cholera (Vibrio cholerae). Amoebiasis causes bloody diarrhea; typhoid fever has fever and constipation; filariasis affects lymphatic system.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the pathogenesis of this problem?
options: Invades colonic mucosa and destroys it
Elaboration of an enterotoxin which acts on bowel mucosal cells
Presence of a secretory peptide from the bacteria
Presence of a superantigen in the patient’s cells

rationale.text: Cholera toxin (an enterotoxin) activates adenylate cyclase in intestinal mucosal cells, causing massive secretion of fluid and electrolytes (rice-water stools). The organism does not invade the mucosa.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the organism involved?

rationale.text: Vibrio cholerae is the causative organism of cholera. Rotavirus causes viral gastroenteritis (children); Giardia causes giardiasis; Salmonella causes typhoid or gastroenteritis.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 4 – A 72-year old preacher developed grouped vesicles in his left flexural thigh radiating to the left side of his abdomen. The vesicles followed the dermatomal distribution of the skin. He consulted the clinic on the third day of his lesions because vesicles were increasing, associated with intense itching, burning and sharp pain. Which one is the pathology of Herpes Zoster is NOT TRUE?
options: HZC virus spreads to the lymphatics then follows hematogenous route.
Sensory ganglia contains dense mononuclear infiltrates with intranuclear inclusion within neurons
In the dorsal root ganglion, HZV virus causes cell necrosis and inflammation
Reactivated chicken pox virus infects sensory nerves that carry it to one or more dermatomes

rationale.text: Herpes zoster is caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the dorsal root ganglia, not by spread via lymphatics/hematogenous route. It travels along sensory nerves to the skin.

subject: Pathology
question: Involvement of the trigeminal nerves may cause which complications?

rationale.text: Trigeminal nerve involvement can cause zoster ophthalmicus (eye) and Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy). Encephalitis and myelitis are less common complications.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the pathological danger of developing Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus?
options: Blurring of vision of affected eye

rationale.text: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus can cause corneal involvement and blindness. Blurring of vision is a sign of corneal involvement; tearing and sand-like feeling are symptoms, not the main danger.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 5 - After coming from their PE class, a young high school student from a prominent family decided to end his life. He stayed overnight with the exhaust of his car aircon in full-blast and engine running in an enclosed garage. Patient is at the same time anemic and asthmatic. After 24 hours, they found him dead. After thorough investigation of the cause of death, the hospital physician concluded that the cause of death is which one of the following gases?

rationale.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning from car exhaust in an enclosed space is a common method of suicide. CO binds to hemoglobin with high affinity, causing tissue hypoxia.

subject: Pathology
question: Which one of the following reasons may not be contributory to the demise?
options: Carbon monoxide toxicity is exacerbated by exercise
He may have developed asthmatic attacks due to the fumes and exhaust of the engines
Carbon monoxide binds more to hemoglobin than oxygen leading to reduced oxygen saturation
Cardiac and skeletal muscles begin to breakdown releasing creatinine kinase

rationale.text: Carbon monoxide is odorless and non-irritating, so it does not trigger asthma attacks. The other options are mechanisms of CO toxicity (though exercise would increase CO uptake if still exposed).

subject: Pathology
question: In the garage was also found insecticide sprays used daily to knockout insects. If used cumulatively, this will also knockout humans inhaling this gas causing neurotoxicity. Which of the following is this gas?

rationale.text: Organophosphates are common insecticides that inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing neurotoxicity. Beryllium causes lung disease; methanol causes acidosis; lead causes heavy metal toxicity.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 6 - A 50 year old lady consulted the clinic because of ‘heartburn’, dysphagia and regurgitation of sour-tasting gastric contents. She experienced these symptoms especially when eating certain food. What is the lady having?

rationale.text: Heartburn, dysphagia, and regurgitation of sour-tasting gastric contents are classic symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Hiatal hernia can contribute, but GERD is the primary diagnosis.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the pathogenesis of Gastroesophageal reflux disease?
options: Abrupt increase in intra abdominal pressure
Forceful opening of lower esophageal sphincter
Delayed gastric emptying and increased gastric volume

rationale.text: Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation is the most common cause of GERD. The other options can contribute but are less common.

subject: Pathology
question: Which one does not cause GERD?

rationale.text: Yogurt is not a cause of GERD; it may even be protective. CNS depressants, alcohol, and tobacco can relax the LES and promote reflux.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 7 - During annual school physical examination, 17 years old Greg is observed to have abnormally long legs, small atrophic testes with small penis and lack of deep voice, facial hair and male pubic hair distribution. The doctor is thinking more along the lines of Klinefelter syndrome. What is the chromosomal abnormality for the above condition?
options: 1 X chromosome and no Y chromosome
2 or more X chromosomes and 1 or more Y chromosomes

rationale.text: Klinefelter syndrome is typically 47,XXY (two or more X chromosomes and one or more Y chromosomes). 45,X is Turner syndrome; 46,XY is normal male; 46,XX is normal female.

subject: Pathology
question: Which factor relates to imbalance of sex chromosomes such as in the case of Klinefelter Syndrome?
options: Large amount of genetic material in Y chromosome
Lyonization or inactivation of just one X chromosome
Minimal amount of genetic material in Y chromosome
Lyonization or inactivation of all but one X chromosome

rationale.text: In Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), one X chromosome is inactivated (Lyonization), but the extra X leads to overexpression of genes that escape inactivation, causing hypogonadism.

subject: Pathology
question: The clinical features of Klinefelter Syndrome are variable. Which among these condition features is the only consistent finding in this condition?

rationale.text: Hypogonadism (small atrophic testes, low testosterone) is the only consistent finding in Klinefelter syndrome. Gynecomastia, tall stature, and learning difficulties are variable.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 8 - 2 year old Faye developed pneumonia, severe oral candidiasis, diarrhea and generalized lymphadenopathy. She was confined in the hospital for diagnostic workups and management. What is the FIRST to do for this case?
options: Insert an IV fluid for her diarrhea
Give the proper antibiotics for her pneumonia
Request for CBC and blood chemistry work ups
Do thorough history taking and complete physical exam

rationale.text: In a seriously ill child, the first priority is stabilization: airway, breathing, circulation (IV fluids for dehydration). Antibiotics and workups come after stabilization.

subject: Pathology
question: Which statement is LEAST LIKELY the reason why Faye can develop the devastating effect of HIV?
options: She was always exposed to her infected mother everyday
Her immature immune system had difficulty containing the infection
High risk of the disease progression can occur in the first few years of life
Immune system has not developed at the time of primary infection

rationale.text: The immune system is present at birth, though immature. HIV in children is often due to maternal transmission; the virus has already adapted to the maternal immune system, making it harder for the child's immature immune system to control.

subject: Pathology
question: In how many years is Faye expected to succumb to her illness after the clinical symptoms?

rationale.text: In the absence of effective therapy, about 10-15% of HIV-infected children die within the first year of life. Progression to AIDS is rapid in infants.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 9 - Olan is maintained on a dopamine antagonist to control his hallucinations. After taking his medications, he developed side effects of Parkinson-like symptoms and gynecomastia. Which of the dopamine tracts is involved in the action of dopamine antagonists in controlling hallucination?

rationale.text: Antipsychotics block dopamine in the mesolimbic tract to reduce hallucinations (positive symptoms). Parkinson-like symptoms are from nigrostriatal blockade; gynecomastia is from tuberoinfundibular blockade (hyperprolactinemia).

subject: Pathology
question: In which of the following dopamine tract would antagonism of dopamine lead to Parkinson-like symptoms?

rationale.text: Antagonism of dopamine in the nigrostriatal tract leads to extrapyramidal symptoms (Parkinson-like).

subject: Pathology
question: In which of the dopamine tract would antagonism of dopamine lead to gynecomastia?

rationale.text: Antagonism in the tuberoinfundibular tract increases prolactin, causing gynecomastia.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 10 - A 35-year old office worker developed dysphagia when he takes solid food and liquids. He also had difficulty in belching. More so, he also developed chest pain every time he had the above symptoms. He consulted a physician who suggested a work-upon him as he might be having achalasia. Which one is NOT a characteristic of Achalasia’?

rationale.text: Achalasia is characterized by increased LES tone, incomplete LES relaxation, and aperistalsis. Relaxation during swallowing is a normal function, not a characteristic of achalasia.

subject: Pathology
question: Which one is an important cause of esophageal obstruction caused by impaired smooth muscle relaxation?
options: Release of the vasoactive intestinal peptide
Increased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter
Decreased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter

rationale.text: Increased LES tone causes obstruction and impaired relaxation. VIP promotes relaxation; decreased tone causes reflux; cholinergic signaling stimulates contraction.

subject: Pathology
question: What is the cause of primary achalasia?

rationale.text: The cause of primary achalasia is unknown (idiopathic). It is characterized by degeneration of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, but the etiology is not established.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 11- 32 year-old mother gave birth to a baby boy who had to undergo a pediatric surgery operation because he kept on vomiting all the food that he ate. Radiography showed a thin noncanalized cord replacing a segment of the esophagus causing mechanical obstruction. What is the baby having?

rationale.text: Esophageal atresia is a congenital condition where a segment of the esophagus is absent (noncanalized cord), causing vomiting and feeding difficulties. Achalasia is a motility disorder; hiatal hernia is stomach herniation; diaphragmatic hernia is abdominal organs in thorax.

subject: Pathology
question: Atresia commonly occurs near the tracheal bifurcation. This condition is usually associated with which structure?

rationale.text: Esophageal atresia is commonly associated with a tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF), an abnormal connection between the trachea and esophagus.

subject: Pathology
question: Which condition is NOT a complication of this case?

rationale.text: Diarrhea is not a complication of esophageal atresia. Aspiration, suffocation (from aspiration), and pneumonia are complications due to the TEF.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 12 - A 50 year old construction worker developed hypoesthetic patches over his right lower back and right thigh areas. He consulted the clinic as he had tried different topical applications to treat the lesions which he had been having for almost a year. What pathologic concerns can give rise to the hypoesthesia?
options: Viral organisms that follow the dermatomal distribution of skin
Presence of organisms that may affect the skin and nerve
Application of caustic chemicals that can destroy affected tissues
History of trauma to area that may destroy the involved nerves

rationale.text: Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) affects skin and peripheral nerves, causing hypoesthetic patches. Viral (e.g., herpes zoster) follows dermatomes but is acute; caustic chemicals and trauma are less likely given the chronicity and distribution.

subject: Pathology
question: How can the construction worker get the disease?
options: Inoculation through cut on the skin area
Droplet inhalation from a contaminated person
Ingestion of food and water from an affected person

rationale.text: Leprosy is primarily transmitted via respiratory droplets from untreated lepromatous leprosy patients. Prolonged skin-to-skin contact is also a risk, but droplet inhalation is the main route.

subject: Pathology
question: Skin biopsy was read as presence of:
options: A Grenz zone beneath the epidermal area
Lipid laden and foam cells in specimen slide
A +4 acid fast bacilli on Fite-Faraco stain

rationale.text: Tuberculoid leprosy shows granulomatous infiltrate with histiocytes; lepromatous leprosy shows foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages) and numerous acid-fast bacilli. A +4 AFB on Fite-Faraco is characteristic of lepromatous leprosy.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 13 - Within 5 minutes after a bee sting, Elsie developed breathing difficulty with marked inspiratory stridor from laryngeal edema. She experienced mild urticaria with swelling of her sting hand. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is she manifesting?

rationale.text: Anaphylaxis (bee sting) is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction (IgE-mediated, immediate). Type II is antibody-mediated cytotoxicity; Type III is immune complex; Type IV is delayed-type.

subject: Pathology
question: What type of cell plays a part in this reaction?

rationale.text: Mast cells and basophils are the primary cells in Type I hypersensitivity, releasing histamine and other mediators. Eosinophils are also involved but later; neutrophils and lymphocytes are not primary.

subject: Pathology
question: One of the following statements may NOT be TRUE of Epinephrine in treating this case?
options: In lieu of epinephrine, glucocorticoid is the choice
The reaction is triggered by mast cell bound IgE releasing histamine
Epinephrine is the fastest acting agent to treat life threatening condition
Epinephrine can be given parenterally and easily available as an emergency drug

rationale.text: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis; glucocorticoids are adjunctive, not a substitute. The other statements are true.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 14- Mike, a 62 year old man, presents with a 4-year history of progressive incontinence, decrease in urine stream, terminal dribbling and abdominal straining when urinating. He would need to urinate frequently, even at night, often feeling the urge despite difficulty initiating voiding. Which statement would LEAST describe Mike’s condition?
options: It is characterized by increase in size of the transition zone surrounding the urethra
PSA levels in the condition are 4ng/ml or lower
It is the most common cause of lower urinary tract symptoms in males
Increased gland size compresses urethra, leading to symptoms

rationale.text: In BPH, PSA is often elevated (>4 ng/mL) or in the gray zone. The other statements are true for BPH.

subject: Pathology
question: Which statement is consistent with the pathophysiology of Mike’s condition?
options: It is not influenced by both endogenous and exogenous estrogens
Type II 5-alpha-reductase metabolizes dihydrotestosterone to testosterone
Testosterone binds to androgen receptors in the cell nuclei leading to hyperplasia
It is hormonally influenced by testosterone and dihydrotestosterone

rationale.text: BPH is hormonally influenced by testosterone and its metabolite DHT. Estrogens also play a role; 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to DHT (not vice versa).

subject: Pathology
question: Which would be LEAST likely expected to find in the histologic report of Mike’s condition?
options: Hyperplasia of glandular and stromal tissues with papillary buds
Begins around the urethra where ejaculatory ducts enter prostate
Stromal changes, such as increased smooth muscles, may be present
Interruptions and nicks along the basal cell layer

rationale.text: Interruptions and nicks along the basal cell layer are not typical of BPH; they suggest carcinoma. BPH shows hyperplasia of glands and stroma, often beginning in the transition zone.

subject: Pathology
question: Situation 15- Aling Nilda comes to your clinic worried of a rapidly enlarging mass last month. She claims to have first noted the mass last month. Mass grew from the size of a corn kernel to its protruding size of a calamansi. You are considering Phyllodes tumor for this case. Which of the following statements MOST likely explains the bulbous protrusions commonly present in larger forms of this tumor? Presence of nodules of ____.
options: Normal stroma covered by distorted epithelium
Proliferating stroma covered by distorted epithelium
Normal stroma covered by proliferating epithelium

rationale.text: Phyllodes tumors have bulbous protrusions due to nodules of proliferating stroma covered by epithelium. The stroma is the proliferative component, not the epithelium.

subject: Pathology
question: What statement BEST differentiate Phyllodes tumors from fibroadenoma? Higher cellularity, nuclear polymorphism___.
options: Normal mitotic rate, Stromal overgrowth and infiltrative borders
Normal mitotic rate, stromal infiltration and normal borders
Higher mitotic rate, stromal infiltration and normal borders
Higher mitotic rate, stromal overgrowth and infiltrative borders

rationale.text: Phyllodes tumors are distinguished from fibroadenomas by higher cellularity, higher mitotic rate, nuclear pleomorphism, stromal overgrowth, and infiltrative borders.

subject: Pathology
question: Which statement BEST describes Phyllodes tumor and metastasis? Most Phyllodes tumor are___.
options: Low grade and occasionally recur but do not metastasize
High grade and rarely gives rise to hematogenous metastases
High grade and gives rise to hematogenous metastases
Low grade and occasionally recur and metastasize

rationale.text: Most phyllodes tumors are low-grade, may recur locally, but do not metastasize. High-grade tumors can metastasize hematogenously, but are uncommon.

subject: Pathology
question: A 35-year-old man with tall stature, arachnodactyly, and pectus excavatum is found to have a dilated aortic root. Echocardiography also reveals mitral valve prolapse. Genetic testing identifies a missense mutation. Which of the following pathogenetic mechanisms best explains the excessive TGF-β signaling in this condition?
options: Dominant negative effect of mutant fibrillin-1 on microfibril assembly
Haploinsufficiency of fibrillin-1 leading to reduced extracellular matrix sequestration of TGF-β
Gain-of-function mutation in the TGF-β receptor type II
Loss-of-function mutation in the gene encoding elastin

rationale.text: Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in FBN1 encoding fibrillin-1. The pathogenesis involves both loss of structural integrity and excessive TGF-β signaling. The reduction of fibrillin-1 below a threshold leads to decreased sequestration of TGF-β in the extracellular matrix, resulting in excessive TGF-β activation. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 129: 'Fibrillin-1 controls TGF-β bioavailability; reduced or altered forms give rise to excessive activation of TGF-β.' Buzzwords: tall stature, arachnodactyly, aortic root dilation, mitral valve prolapse. Mnemonic: Fibrillin = F (Fails to sequester TGF-β).

subject: Pathology
question: A newborn is noted to have bilateral ectopia lentis, a high-arched palate, and hyperextensible joints. The parents are phenotypically normal. Which of the following statements best describes the inheritance pattern most likely responsible for this condition?
options: Autosomal recessive inheritance with both parents being carriers
Autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance in the parents
X-linked recessive inheritance with the mother being a carrier
De novo autosomal dominant mutation in the FBN1 gene

rationale.text: The child has Marfan syndrome. Approximately 75% of cases are familial with autosomal dominant inheritance. The remaining 25% arise from de novo mutations in FBN1. The parents being phenotypically normal makes autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance less likely, and de novo mutation is the most plausible explanation. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 129: 'Approximately 75% of cases are familial and transmitted by autosomal dominant inheritance. The remainder are sporadic and arise from de novo mutations.' Buzzwords: bilateral ectopia lentis, high-arched palate, hyperextensible joints.

subject: Pathology
question: A 28-year-old woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presents with easy bruising, hyperextensible skin, and joint hypermobility. She is planning a pregnancy and is concerned about inheritance. Which of the following is the most common inheritance pattern for the classic type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?

rationale.text: Classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is most commonly caused by mutations in COL5A1 or COL5A2 and follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. The kyphoscoliotic type is autosomal recessive. The hypermobility type has an unknown genetic basis. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, Table 5.5: 'Classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: autosomal dominant, COL5A1 or COL5A2 mutations.' Buzzwords: easy bruising, hyperextensible skin, joint hypermobility. Mnemonic: EDS classic = D (Dominant).

subject: Pathology
question: A 45-year-old man with a history of spontaneous colonic rupture and arterial dissection is diagnosed with the vascular type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Which of the following collagen types is most directly affected by the underlying mutation?

rationale.text: The vascular type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (type IV) results from mutations in COL3A1 encoding type III collagen. Type III collagen is particularly abundant in blood vessels and intestines, explaining the predisposition to spontaneous arterial rupture and colonic perforation. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 130: 'The vascular type of EDS typically results from abnormalities of type III collagen.' Buzzwords: spontaneous colonic rupture, arterial dissection. Mnemonic: Vascular EDS = V (type III collagen in Vessels).

subject: Pathology
question: A 55-year-old woman with familial hypercholesterolemia presents with a xanthoma on her Achilles tendon. Her LDL cholesterol level is markedly elevated. Mutational analysis reveals a defect in the LDL receptor that prevents its transport from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus. This defect corresponds to which class of LDL receptor mutation?

rationale.text: LDL receptor mutations are classified into six classes based on functional defects. Class II mutations (the most common) encode LDL receptors that are synthesized but accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum due to misfolding or C-terminal truncations, preventing their transport to the Golgi apparatus. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, Fig. 5.9: 'Class II mutations are fairly common; they encode LDL receptor proteins that accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum because of C-terminal truncations or folding defects that block transport to the Golgi complex.' Buzzwords: xanthoma, marked LDL elevation, ER retention. Mnemonic: Class II = ER (Endoplasmic Reticulum retention).

subject: Pathology
question: A 6-month-old infant of Ashkenazi Jewish descent presents with progressive motor deterioration, loss of milestones, and a cherry-red spot on the macula. Enzyme assay confirms deficiency of hexosaminidase A. Which of the following is the most common molecular mechanism underlying this deficiency?
options: Four-base pair insertion causing a frameshift mutation
Single-base substitution creating a premature stop codon
Large deletion encompassing the entire HEXA gene
Trinucleotide repeat expansion in the 5' untranslated region

rationale.text: Tay-Sachs disease in Ashkenazi Jewish individuals is most commonly caused by a four-base pair insertion in the HEXA gene, leading to a frameshift mutation and premature stop codon. This is the classic mutation in this population and has a founder effect. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, Fig. 5.4: 'Four-base pair insertion in the hexosaminidase A gene, leading to a frameshift mutation, is the major cause of Tay-Sachs disease in Ashkenazi Jewish people.' Buzzwords: Ashkenazi Jewish, cherry-red spot, motor deterioration, hexosaminidase A. Mnemonic: Tay-Sachs = T (Four-base insertion, Truncated protein).

subject: Pathology
question: A 2-year-old child presents with hepatosplenomegaly, an abnormal gait, and a cherry-red spot on the macula. Sphingomyelinase activity is markedly reduced. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

rationale.text: Niemann-Pick disease type A is caused by deficiency of sphingomyelinase, leading to accumulation of sphingomyelin in the liver, spleen, and nervous system. It presents with hepatosplenomegaly, cherry-red spot, and progressive neurodegeneration. Gaucher disease has no cherry-red spot in type I. Tay-Sachs has hepatosplenomegaly but no sphingomyelinase deficiency. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 136: 'Niemann-Pick disease types A and B are characterized by lysosomal accumulation of sphingomyelin due to an inherited deficiency of sphingomyelinase.' Buzzwords: hepatosplenomegaly, cherry-red spot, sphingomyelinase deficiency. Mnemonic: Niemann-Pick = N (No sphingomyelinase).

subject: Pathology
question: A 40-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish man presents with bone pain, thrombocytopenia, and an enlarged spleen. Bone marrow biopsy shows macrophages with cytoplasm resembling crumpled tissue paper. Which of the following is the most likely underlying enzyme deficiency?

rationale.text: Gaucher disease type I is caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency, resulting in accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages (Gaucher cells). Gaucher cells have characteristic cytoplasm resembling crumpled tissue paper. The patient is Ashkenazi Jewish, the population with the highest prevalence of type I Gaucher disease. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 137: 'Gaucher cells have a fibrillary type of cytoplasm likened to crumpled tissue paper.' Buzzwords: bone pain, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, crumpled tissue paper cytoplasm. Mnemonic: Gaucher = G (Glucocerebrosidase deficiency).

subject: Pathology
question: A 5-year-old child with coarse facial features, corneal clouding, and hepatosplenomegaly is diagnosed with Hurler syndrome. Which of the following is the most likely mode of inheritance?

rationale.text: Hurler syndrome (MPS I-H) is caused by deficiency of α-L-iduronidase and is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Hunter syndrome (MPS II) is X-linked recessive and is characterized by the absence of corneal clouding and a milder course.
