Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 138: 'All the MPSs are inherited as autosomal recessive traits except Hunter syndrome, which is an X-linked recessive trait.' Buzzwords: coarse facial features, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly. Mnemonic: Hurler = H (Hurler is autosomal recessive, Hunter is X-linked).

subject: Pathology
question: A 2-year-old child presents with hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and failure to thrive. Liver biopsy shows marked glycogen accumulation in hepatocytes. Laboratory studies reveal elevated uric acid and triglycerides. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible for this presentation?

rationale.text: Von Gierke disease (type I glycogen storage disease) is caused by deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase. The inability to convert glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose leads to hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, Table 5.7: 'Hepatorenal—von Gierke disease (type I): Glucose-6-phosphatase; hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia.' Buzzwords: hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, elevated uric acid and triglycerides. Mnemonic: Von Gierke = G (Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency).

subject: Pathology
question: A young adult presents with exercise-induced muscle cramps, myoglobinuria, and failure of blood lactate levels to rise after exercise. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible?

rationale.text: McArdle disease (type V glycogen storage disease) is caused by muscle phosphorylase deficiency. It presents with exercise-induced muscle cramps and myoglobinuria, and blood lactate does not rise after exercise. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, Table 5.7: 'McArdle disease (type V): Muscle phosphorylase; painful cramps associated with strenuous exercise; myoglobinuria; muscular exercise fails to raise lactate level in venous blood.' Buzzwords: exercise-induced cramps, myoglobinuria, no lactate rise. Mnemonic: McArdle = M (Muscle phosphorylase, Myoglobinuria).

subject: Pathology
question: A 3-year-old child with Pompe disease is found to have massive cardiomegaly. Which of the following best explains the molecular mechanism of this disease?
options: Deficiency of lysosomal acid α-glucosidase with glycogen accumulation in lysosomes
Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase with impaired glycogen breakdown
Deficiency of muscle phosphorylase with impaired glycolysis
Deficiency of branching enzyme with abnormal glycogen structure

rationale.text: Pompe disease (type II glycogen storage disease) is caused by deficiency of lysosomal acid α-glucosidase (acid maltase). Glycogen accumulates in lysosomes, leading to massive cardiomegaly, muscle hypotonia, and cardiorespiratory failure in the infantile form. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, Table 5.7: 'Generalized glycogenosis—Pompe disease (type II): Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase; massive cardiomegaly.' Buzzwords: Pompe disease, cardiomegaly, lysosomal glycogen accumulation. Mnemonic: Pompe = P (Pump failure from lysosomal glycogen).

subject: Pathology
question: A 6-year-old girl who was developing normally presents with loss of acquired milestones, microcephaly, and repetitive hand-wringing movements. She has a history of seizures and ataxia. Which of the following genes is most likely mutated in this patient?

rationale.text: Rett syndrome is caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene (methyl CpG-binding protein 2) and presents in girls with normal early development followed by regression, loss of speech, microcephaly, and stereotypical hand-wringing. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 141: 'Rett syndrome is an X-linked condition affecting 1 in 10,000 female births and caused by mutations in the DNA methyl-CpG reader (MECP2).' Buzzwords: microcephaly, hand-wringing, loss of milestones, female. Mnemonic: Rett = R (Regression, hand-wringing).

subject: Pathology
question: A newborn with microcephaly, hypotonia, and a high-pitched cry is found to have a deletion of the proximal long arm of chromosome 5. Which of the following is the most appropriate term for this chromosomal abnormality?

rationale.text: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by an interstitial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-). An interstitial deletion occurs when there are two breaks within a chromosome arm, followed by loss of material between the breaks and fusion of the broken ends. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 145: 'Interstitial deletions occur when there are two breaks within a chromosome arm, followed by loss of the chromosomal material between the breaks and fusion of the broken ends.' Buzzwords: microcephaly, hypotonia, high-pitched cry, deletion of chromosome 5. Mnemonic: Cri-du-chat = C (Cry like a cat).

subject: Pathology
question: A 25-year-old pregnant woman at 16 weeks gestation undergoes amniocentesis due to advanced maternal age. The karyotype of the fetus is 47,XX,+21. Which of the following is the most common mechanism responsible for this chromosomal abnormality?
options: Mosaicism from a postzygotic mitotic error

rationale.text: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is caused by meiotic nondisjunction in 95% of cases, with the extra chromosome 21 being of maternal origin in 95% of those cases. Nondisjunction during maternal meiosis I is the most common mechanism. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 146: 'Maternal age has a strong influence on the incidence of trisomy 21… in 95% of the cases, the extra chromosome 21 is of maternal origin.' Buzzwords: advanced maternal age, trisomy 21, nondisjunction. Mnemonic: Trisomy 21 = M (Maternal nondisjunction).

subject: Pathology
question: A newborn with Down syndrome is found to have an atrioventricular septal defect. Which of the following is the most common congenital heart defect in patients with trisomy 21?

rationale.text: Atrioventricular septal defects are the most common congenital heart defects in Down syndrome, accounting for 43% of cases. Ventricular septal defects (32%) and atrial septal defects (19%) are also common but less frequent. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 147: 'The most frequent forms of congenital heart disease in Down syndrome are atrioventricular septal defects constituting 43% of cases.' Buzzwords: Down syndrome, congenital heart disease. Mnemonic: Down = A (AVSD is most common).

subject: Pathology
question: A 40-year-old woman with Down syndrome presents with progressive memory loss and confusion. Neuroimaging reveals cortical atrophy. Which of the following genes, when overexpressed due to trisomy 21, is most directly implicated in the early development of Alzheimer disease in these patients?

rationale.text: The APP gene (amyloid-beta precursor protein) is located on chromosome 21. Overexpression of APP in trisomy 21 leads to increased production of amyloid-beta, which contributes to the early development of Alzheimer disease in patients with Down syndrome. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 147: 'Included among these [overexpressed genes] is the gene for amyloid-beta precursor protein (APP).' Buzzwords: Down syndrome, Alzheimer disease, amyloid-beta. Mnemonic: APP = A (Amyloid precursor protein).

subject: Pathology
question: A child with DiGeorge syndrome presents with tetany, congenital heart disease, and recurrent infections. Which of the following is the most likely genetic abnormality?

rationale.text: DiGeorge syndrome is caused by a deletion of chromosome 22q11.2, resulting in thymic hypoplasia (T-cell immunodeficiency), parathyroid hypoplasia (hypocalcemia), and cardiac outflow tract defects. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 147: 'Chromosome 22q11.2 deletion syndrome encompasses a spectrum of disorders… includes DiGeorge syndrome (thymic hypoplasia… parathyroid hypoplasia… cardiac malformations).' Buzzwords: DiGeorge, tetany, congenital heart disease, recurrent infections. Mnemonic: DiGeorge = D (Deletion 22q11.2).

subject: Pathology
question: A child with a submicroscopic deletion of chromosome 22q11.2 presents with a cardiac outflow tract defect, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia. Which of the following genes is most closely associated with the phenotypic features of this syndrome?

rationale.text: TBX1 is a T-box transcription factor located in the 22q11.2 region. It is expressed in the pharyngeal mesenchyme and endodermal pouches from which facial structures, thymus, and parathyroid are derived. TBX1 is most closely associated with the phenotypic features of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 148: 'Among these, TBX1, a T-box transcription factor, is most closely associated with the phenotypic features of this syndrome.' Buzzwords: 22q11.2 deletion, cardiac outflow tract defect, cleft palate, hypocalcemia. Mnemonic: TBX1 = T (T-box transcription factor).

subject: Pathology
question: A 16-year-old boy presents with tall stature, small atrophic testes, gynecomastia, and learning difficulties. Karyotype analysis reveals 47,XXY. Which of the following is the most consistent clinical finding in this condition?

rationale.text: In Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), hypogonadism is the only consistent clinical finding. Gynecomastia, tall stature, and learning difficulties are variable features, but small atrophic testes (hypogonadism) are present in all patients. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 150: 'The clinical features of Klinefelter syndrome are quite variable, the only consistent finding being hypogonadism.' Buzzwords: tall stature, small atrophic testes, gynecomastia, XXY. Mnemonic: Klinefelter = K (Keep hypogonadism constant).

subject: Pathology
question: A 30-year-old woman with primary amenorrhea, short stature, webbed neck, and a shield-like chest is diagnosed with Turner syndrome. Which of the following is the most common cardiovascular abnormality in this condition?

rationale.text: Coarctation of the aorta is the most common cardiovascular abnormality in Turner syndrome, along with bicuspid aortic valve. Aortic dissection is a complication of aortic root dilation, which occurs in 30% of cases but is less common than coarctation. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 151: 'Congenital heart disease… Left-sided cardiovascular abnormalities, particularly preductal coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve, are seen most frequently.' Buzzwords: Turner syndrome, webbed neck, short stature, primary amenorrhea. Mnemonic: Turner = C (Coarctation of aorta).

subject: Pathology
question: A newborn female with Turner syndrome presents with swelling of the dorsum of the hands and feet and a cystic hygroma of the neck. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the lymphedema in this patient?
options: Lymphatic stasis from distended lymphatic channels

rationale.text: Lymphedema in Turner syndrome results from lymphatic stasis due to distended lymphatic channels. The swelling of the dorsum of the hands and feet and cystic hygroma of the neck are due to lymph accumulation in the lymphatic vessels. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 151: 'The most severely affected patients generally present during infancy with edema of the dorsum of the hand and foot due to lymph stasis and sometimes swelling of the nape of the neck.' Buzzwords: cystic hygroma, lymphedema, Turner syndrome. Mnemonic: Turner = L (Lymphatic stasis).

subject: Pathology
question: A child with Prader-Willi syndrome presents with hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, and hypogonadism. Genetic analysis reveals an interstitial deletion of chromosome 15q11.2-q13. Which of the following best explains why this deletion results in Prader-Willi syndrome?
options: The deleted region is paternally imprinted, so only the maternal allele is active
The deleted region is maternally imprinted, so only the paternal allele is active
Both maternal and paternal alleles are equally expressed in this region
The deletion disrupts a gene that is only expressed in males

rationale.text: In Prader-Willi syndrome, the region 15q11.2-q13 is imprinted on the maternal chromosome (maternally imprinted), meaning only the paternal allele is active. Deletion of the paternal chromosome results in loss of function of genes in this region. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, Fig. 5.31: 'A set of genes in the PWS region on maternal chromosome 15q12 is imprinted (and hence silenced), and thus, the only functional genes are provided by the paternal chromosome. When these are lost because of a deletion, the person develops Prader-Willi syndrome.' Buzzwords: Prader-Willi, hyperphagia, obesity, hypotonia. Mnemonic: Prader-Willi = P (Paternal loss).

subject: Pathology
question: A child with Angelman syndrome presents with severe intellectual disability, ataxic gait, seizures, and inappropriate laughter. Genetic analysis reveals a deletion of the same chromosomal region as Prader-Willi syndrome. Which of the following genes is most directly responsible for Angelman syndrome?

rationale.text: Angelman syndrome is caused by loss of function of the UBE3A gene, which is imprinted on the paternal chromosome and expressed only from the maternal allele. Deletion of the maternal chromosome results in loss of UBE3A expression. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 157: 'A distinct gene (UBE3A) that also maps to the same region of chromosome 15 is imprinted on the paternal chromosome. Only the maternally derived copy of this gene is normally active.' Buzzwords: Angelman, ataxic gait, inappropriate laughter, seizures. Mnemonic: Angelman = U (UBE3A).

subject: Pathology
question: A child with Angelman syndrome is found to have two paternal copies of chromosome 15 and no maternal copy. Which of the following terms best describes this mechanism?

rationale.text: Uniparental disomy refers to the inheritance of both chromosomes of a pair from one parent. In Angelman syndrome, uniparental disomy of paternal chromosome 15 (two paternal copies, no maternal copy) results in no functional UBE3A, causing the syndrome. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 157: 'Inheritance of both chromosomes of a pair from one parent is called uniparental disomy.' Buzzwords: Angelman syndrome, two paternal copies. Mnemonic: Uniparental disomy = U (Both from one parent).

subject: Pathology
question: A 2-year-old boy with severe intellectual disability, macroorchidism, and a long face with large everted ears is diagnosed with fragile X syndrome. Which of the following is the most common cause of intellectual disability in males?

rationale.text: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and the second most common overall cause after Down syndrome. It is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability in males. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 153: 'FXS is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability in males and the second most common overall cause of intellectual disability after Down syndrome.' Buzzwords: macroorchidism, long face, large everted ears, intellectual disability. Mnemonic: Fragile X = F (First in males).

subject: Pathology
question: A 35-year-old man with a family history of fragile X syndrome is a carrier of a premutation. His sister, also a carrier, has two children: a son with fragile X syndrome and a daughter who is unaffected. Which of the following best explains why the son is affected while the daughter is not?
options: The premutation expanded to a full mutation during spermatogenesis
The premutation expanded to a full mutation during oogenesis
The son inherited the premutation from his father
The daughter has favorable X-inactivation patterns

rationale.text: In fragile X syndrome, the premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) expands to a full mutation (>230 repeats) during oogenesis (not spermatogenesis). When a carrier female transmits the premutation, there is a high probability of dramatic amplification, leading to affected male offspring. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 154: 'During oogenesis, but not spermatogenesis, premutations can be converted to mutations by triplet-repeat amplification.' Buzzwords: premutation, carrier female, affected son. Mnemonic: Fragile X = O (Oogenesis expansion).

subject: Pathology
question: A 60-year-old man with a history of being a carrier of the fragile X premutation presents with progressive intention tremor and cerebellar ataxia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

rationale.text: Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) is a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome that affects approximately 50% of male premutation carriers in their sixth decade, presenting with intention tremor and cerebellar ataxia. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 156: 'Approximately 50% of premutation-carrying males (transmitting males) exhibit a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome starting in their sixth decade… fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia.' Buzzwords: tremor, ataxia, premutation carrier. Mnemonic: FXTAS = T (Tremor and Ataxia Syndrome).

subject: Pathology
question: A 20-year-old man with progressive visual loss in both eyes is diagnosed with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of this condition?

rationale.text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA and exhibits maternal inheritance. The disorder is transmitted from mothers to all their offspring, but only females transmit the mutation further. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 156: 'A feature unique to mtDNA is maternal inheritance… mothers transmit mtDNA to all their offspring; females, but not males, transmit the DNA further to their progeny.' Buzzwords: progressive visual loss, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. Mnemonic: Leber = M (Maternal inheritance).

subject: Pathology
question: A 45-year-old man with a family history of Huntington disease undergoes genetic testing and is found to have an expanded CAG repeat. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism by which this mutation causes disease?
options: Loss of function due to transcriptional silencing
Toxic gain of function due to polyglutamine expansion
Toxic gain of function mediated by mutant RNA

rationale.text: Huntington disease is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the coding region of the HTT gene, leading to a polyglutamine expansion. This results in a toxic gain of function, where the mutant huntingtin protein aggregates, interferes with transcription, and causes neurodegeneration. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 153: 'A toxic gain of function by alterations of protein structure, as in Huntington disease… the expansions occur in the coding regions of the genes.' Buzzwords: CAG repeat, Huntington disease, polyglutamine. Mnemonic: Huntington = P (Polyglutamine expansion).

subject: Pathology
question: A 40-year-old man with a family history of spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 is found to have a CAG repeat expansion. Which of the following is the most common morphologic feature of disorders caused by polyglutamine expansions?
options: Intranuclear inclusions of aggregated mutant protein
Demyelination of the spinal cord tracts

rationale.text: Polyglutamine diseases (including Huntington disease and spinocerebellar ataxias) are characterized by the accumulation of aggregated mutant proteins in intranuclear inclusions. These inclusions are a morphologic hallmark of this group of disorders. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 153: 'A morphologic hallmark of these diseases is the accumulation of aggregated mutant proteins in large intranuclear inclusions.' Buzzwords: polyglutamine expansion, neurodegeneration. Mnemonic: Polyglutamine = I (Intranuclear inclusions).

subject: Pathology
question: A 5-year-old child with severe intellectual disability and a history of seizures is found to have a microdeletion on chromosome 15q11.2-q13. The deletion is on the maternal chromosome. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

rationale.text: Angelman syndrome is caused by deletion of the maternal chromosome 15q11.2-q13, resulting in loss of UBE3A (which is imprinted on the paternal chromosome). Prader-Willi syndrome results from deletion of the paternal chromosome in the same region. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, Fig. 5.31: 'Angelman syndrome… patients are born with a deletion of the same chromosomal region derived from their mothers.' Buzzwords: intellectual disability, ataxia, seizures, maternal deletion. Mnemonic: Angelman = M (Maternal deletion).

subject: Pathology
question: A 30-year-old woman with a family history of breast and ovarian cancer undergoes genetic testing and is found to have a mutation in the BRCA1 gene. Which of the following is the most appropriate term for this type of mutation?

rationale.text: A germline mutation is present in the egg or sperm and is transmitted to all cells of the offspring. BRCA1 mutations associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer are germline mutations. Somatic mutations are acquired in tissues and are not inherited. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 123: 'Mutations transmitted by germ cells to progeny can give rise to inherited diseases.' Buzzwords: family history, BRCA1, breast and ovarian cancer. Mnemonic: Germline = G (Genetic, inherited).

subject: Pathology
question: A 65-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia is found to have the Philadelphia chromosome. Which of the following is the most appropriate technique for detecting this translocation?

rationale.text: The Philadelphia chromosome is a translocation t(9;22) between the BCR and ABL genes. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is commonly used to detect this translocation, especially with break-apart probes or dual-fusion probes. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 161: 'FISH is used to detect variable partner translocations… BCR-ABL fusion genes in chronic myeloid leukemia.' Buzzwords: Philadelphia chromosome, CML, translocation. Mnemonic: FISH = F (Fusion detection).

subject: Pathology
question: A 50-year-old woman with a history of smoking presents with hemoptysis. CT reveals a lung mass. Biopsy shows adenocarcinoma. Sequencing reveals a mutation in the EGFR gene. Which of the following is the most appropriate indication for genetic testing of this mutation?

rationale.text: EGFR mutations in lung adenocarcinoma are predictive markers for response to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g., erlotinib, osimertinib). Testing is performed to select patients who will benefit from targeted therapy. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 160: 'Identification of specific genetic alterations that can direct therapeutic choices (e.g., mutation of EGFR… in lung cancer).' Buzzwords: EGFR mutation, lung adenocarcinoma, targeted therapy. Mnemonic: EGFR = E (Efficacy of targeted therapy).

subject: Pathology
question: A 60-year-old man with a history of chronic myeloid leukemia is being evaluated for minimal residual disease after treatment. Which of the following techniques is most appropriate for detecting low levels of residual leukemic cells?

rationale.text: Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) is used to monitor minimal residual disease by detecting low levels of BCR-ABL transcripts in patients with chronic myeloid leukemia. qPCR is highly sensitive and can detect disease burden at levels not detectable by other methods. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 161: 'Real-time PCR… monitor the burden of disease in cancers bearing characteristic genetic lesions… level of BCR-ABL fusion mRNA transcripts in patients with CML.' Buzzwords: minimal residual disease, CML, BCR-ABL. Mnemonic: qPCR = Q (Quantify residual disease).

subject: Pathology
question: A newborn with multiple congenital anomalies is found to have a karyotype of 47,XX,+18. Which of the following is the most appropriate term for this chromosomal abnormality?

rationale.text: Aneuploidy refers to a chromosome number that is not an exact multiple of the haploid number (23). Trisomy 18 (47,XX,+18) is a form of aneuploidy. Euploidy is an exact multiple of 23; polyploidy is a multiple greater than diploid; mosaicism is the presence of two or more cell populations. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 145: 'If an error occurs in meiosis or mitosis and a cell acquires a chromosome complement that is not an exact multiple of 23, it is referred to as aneuploidy.' Buzzwords: trisomy 18, 47 chromosomes. Mnemonic: Aneuploidy = A (Abnormal number).

subject: Pathology
question: A 30-year-old woman with a history of pregnancy loss is found to have a balanced reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 2 and 5. Which of the following is the most significant risk associated with this finding?
options: Having children with unbalanced chromosomal complements

rationale.text: A balanced reciprocal translocation carrier has a normal phenotype but is at increased risk for producing unbalanced gametes, leading to spontaneous abortion or the birth of a child with congenital anomalies. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 145: 'A balanced translocation carrier… is at increased risk for producing abnormal gametes… Subsequent fertilization… would lead to the formation of an abnormal (unbalanced) zygote, resulting in spontaneous abortion or birth of a malformed child.' Buzzwords: balanced translocation, carrier. Mnemonic: Balanced translocation = U (Unbalanced progeny risk).

subject: Pathology
question: A patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia is treated with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA). This treatment is effective because the leukemia cells harbor a specific chromosomal translocation. Which of the following techniques is most appropriate for confirming this translocation?
options: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with a break-apart probe

rationale.text: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is associated with the t(15;17) translocation involving the PML and RARA genes. FISH with a break-apart probe can detect this translocation even when the partner is unknown or when conventional karyotyping is not informative. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 161: 'FISH can be used in certain circumstances when rapid diagnosis is essential (e.g., when deciding to treat a patient with suspected acute promyelocytic leukemia with retinoic acid).' Buzzwords: APL, ATRA, translocation. Mnemonic: FISH = F (Fast diagnosis).

subject: Pathology
question: A 60-year-old man with a history of smoking presents with hematuria. Cystoscopy reveals a bladder mass. Biopsy shows urothelial carcinoma. Sequencing of the tumor reveals a high tumor mutational burden (TMB). Which of the following is the most likely clinical significance of this finding?
options: Improved response to immune checkpoint inhibitors

rationale.text: High tumor mutational burden (TMB) is associated with improved response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., pembrolizumab). Cancers with many mutations are more likely to produce neoantigens that can be recognized by the immune system. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 165: 'Cancers with high tumor mutational burden (TMB) or acquired defects in mismatch repair genes that lead to microsatellite instability (MSI) tend to be responsive to immune checkpoint inhibitors.' Buzzwords: high TMB, bladder cancer, immune checkpoint inhibitors. Mnemonic: TMB = T (Target for immunotherapy).

subject: Pathology
question: A 45-year-old woman with a family history of early-onset breast cancer undergoes genetic testing and is found to have a mutation in the TP53 gene. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome

rationale.text: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germline mutations in TP53 and is characterized by early-onset breast cancer, sarcomas, brain tumors, and adrenal cortical carcinomas. Lynch syndrome involves mismatch repair genes; familial adenomatous polyposis involves APC; hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome involves BRCA1/2. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 160: 'Inherited cancer syndromes (triggered by either family history or an unusual cancer presentation, such as multiple cancer types or unusually young age at diagnosis).' Buzzwords: TP53 mutation, early-onset breast cancer. Mnemonic: Li-Fraumeni = T (TP53).

subject: Pathology
question: A 25-year-old man with a history of multiple café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules is diagnosed with neurofibromatosis type 1. Which of the following is the most likely inheritance pattern?

rationale.text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17. It presents with café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, Table 5.1: 'Nervous: Neurofibromatosis.' Buzzwords: café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules. Mnemonic: NF1 = A (Autosomal dominant).

subject: Pathology
question: A 55-year-old man with a history of Huntington disease in his family undergoes predictive genetic testing. The test reveals a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Which of the following is the most appropriate counseling message regarding the risk of transmitting the mutation to his children?
options: All children will inherit the mutation
Each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutation
Only male children are at risk
Only female children are at risk

rationale.text: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant disorder. Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutant allele and developing the disease. The trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene is transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 125: 'When an affected and an unaffected person reproduce, each child has one chance in two of inheriting the mutated allele from the affected parent and developing the disease.' Buzzwords: Huntington disease, CAG repeat, autosomal dominant. Mnemonic: Huntington = H (Half the children affected).

subject: Pathology
question: A 30-year-old woman with a family history of hemophilia A undergoes genetic counseling. She is found to be a carrier of the mutated gene. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement regarding the risk of her sons being affected?
options: Each son has a 50% chance of being affected
Neither sons nor daughters are at risk

rationale.text: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder. A carrier female has a 50% chance of passing the mutant X chromosome to each child. Sons who inherit the mutant X chromosome will be affected; daughters who inherit it will be carriers. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 126: 'Sons of heterozygous women have one chance in two of inheriting the mutant allele and being affected by the disease.' Buzzwords: hemophilia A, carrier female, X-linked recessive. Mnemonic: X-linked recessive = S (Sons at 50% risk).

subject: Pathology
question: A 40-year-old man with a history of familial hypercholesterolemia is found to have a mutation in the PCSK9 gene. Which of the following is the most likely effect of this mutation?

rationale.text: PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) reduces expression of the LDL receptor by binding to it and inducing a conformational change marking it for degradation in lysosomes. Activating mutations in PCSK9 increase LDL receptor degradation, reducing LDL clearance and raising serum cholesterol. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 131: 'PCSK9 reduces expression of the LDL receptor by directly binding the protein and inducing a conformational change marking it for degradation in lysosomes in lieu of receptor recycling.' Buzzwords: PCSK9, increased LDL receptor degradation. Mnemonic: PCSK9 = P (Promotes degradation).

subject: Pathology
question: A 6-month-old infant with Tay-Sachs disease is found to have a mutation in the HEXA gene. Which of the following is the most likely origin of the mutation in the Ashkenazi Jewish population?

rationale.text: Tay-Sachs disease is more common in the Ashkenazi Jewish population due to a founder effect, where a mutation that arose in a small population is enriched in descendants due to genetic drift and population isolation. The specific mutation (four-base insertion) originated from a common ancestor. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 135: 'This disease is especially prevalent among Jewish people, particularly among those of Eastern European (Ashkenazic) origin, in whom a carrier rate of 1 in 30 has been reported.' Buzzwords: Ashkenazi Jewish, Tay-Sachs, founder effect. Mnemonic: Founder effect = F (Frequency in founders).

subject: Pathology
question: A 35-year-old man with a history of myotonic dystrophy presents with progressive muscle weakness and myotonia. Genetic testing reveals a CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this disease?
options: Loss of function due to transcriptional silencing
Toxic gain of function due to mutant RNA
Toxic gain of function due to polyglutamine expansion

rationale.text: Myotonic dystrophy is caused by a CTG repeat expansion in the noncoding region of the DMPK gene. The expanded repeat leads to a toxic gain of function mediated by mutant RNA, which sequesters RNA-binding proteins and impairs their function. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 153: 'A toxic gain of function mediated by RNA as is seen in fragile X-associated tremor/ ataxia syndrome… noncoding parts of the gene are affected.' Buzzwords: myotonic dystrophy, CTG repeat, RNA toxicity. Mnemonic: Myotonic dystrophy = R (RNA toxicity).

subject: Pathology
question: A 60-year-old man with a history of a 40-pack-year smoking history is diagnosed with small cell lung carcinoma. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the TP53 gene. Which of the following is the most likely origin of this mutation?

rationale.text: TP53 mutations in small cell lung carcinoma are typically somatic mutations acquired from exposure to tobacco carcinogens. They are not inherited and are present only in the tumor tissue. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 123: 'Mutations that arise in somatic cells understandably do not cause hereditary diseases.' Buzzwords: smoking, lung cancer, TP53 mutation. Mnemonic: Somatic = S (Smoking-related).

subject: Pathology
question: A 30-year-old woman with a history of early menopause is found to have a premutation in the FMR1 gene. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

rationale.text: Fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency (FXPOI) affects approximately 20% of female premutation carriers and presents with premature ovarian failure (before age 40), menstrual irregularities, and decreased fertility. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 156: 'Approximately 20% of females carrying the premutation (carrier females) have premature ovarian failure (before the age of 40 years).' Buzzwords: premutation, early menopause, FMR1. Mnemonic: FXPOI = O (Ovarian insufficiency).

subject: Pathology
question: A 25-year-old man with a history of progressive visual loss and cardiac conduction defects is diagnosed with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. Which of the following is the most likely molecular mechanism of this disease?
options: Mutation in a nuclear gene affecting mitochondrial protein import
Mutation in mitochondrial DNA encoding a subunit of the respiratory chain
Trinucleotide repeat expansion in a mitochondrial gene

rationale.text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA that encode subunits of the respiratory chain enzymes (Complex I). These mutations impair oxidative phosphorylation, leading to neurodegeneration in tissues with high energy demands. Robbins 10th Ed, Chapter 5, p. 156: 'Because mtDNA encodes enzymes involved in oxidative phosphorylation, mutations affecting these genes exert their deleterious effects primarily on the organs most dependent on oxidative phosphorylation such as the central nervous system.' Buzzwords: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, mitochondrial DNA, visual loss. Mnemonic: Leber = M (Mitochondrial mutation).
